mainTopic: אשו משום חציו and טמון באש, and the case of the dog, the cake and the coal
overview: The amud opens as the גמרא finishes a proof from the פסוק that a person's fire counts like his own arrows (אשו משום חציו). אביי then asks a question: if fire is like arrows, how can the Torah ever exempt hidden items (טמון) burned in a fire? His answer is a case where the fence fell for some other reason, so the 'arrows' ran out. The גמרא rejects that answer, because then open items (גלוי) would be exempt too. Instead it says that even the 'arrows' view agrees that fire also counts as one's property (ממונו), and that is where the exemption for טמון applies. The two views then differ only on the four extra payments for injuring a person. Next the גמרא returns to the משנה of the dog that carried off a cake with a coal on it. It explains that the dog's owner pays, that the coal's owner guarded properly, and that the dog dug its way in. רב מרי learns from this that dogs normally dig under doors. Finally, the dog must have eaten the cake on its owner's own stack, and the גמרא starts using this to settle a question about a cow's mouth, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The verse moves from damage by property to damage by the person
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק about fire starts by describing damage done by a person's property and ends by describing damage done by the person himself. This teaches that fire counts like his own arrows.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse begins with damage done by one's property and ends with damage done by one's body, to teach you that his fire is like his arrows.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a proof that started on the previous amud. The way the פסוק about fire is worded shows that אשו משום חציו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק first says 'if a fire goes out', which sounds like the fire is just his property doing damage. But it ends with 'the one who lit the fire shall pay', which treats the person himself as the one doing the damage. Putting the two together teaches that his fire counts as his own direct action, just like arrows he shoots.

keyTerms.meaning: Damage done by a person's property (like his animal or pit)
Damage done by the person's own body or direct action
His fire counts like his arrows, meaning his own direct action

steps.whatToRemember: According to this view, a person who lights a fire is responsible as if he shot arrows himself (אשו משום חציו).
steps.whyThisMatters: This idea sets up the whole question that follows: if fire is like arrows, every rule about fire has to fit that picture.

phrases.english: [The verse opened] with damage done by his property,
phrases.notes: The פסוק here is שמות 22:5, which starts with a fire going out.

phrases.english: and it ended with damage done by his body;
phrases.notes: The end of the פסוק says 'the one who lit the fire shall pay', putting the focus on the person himself.

phrases.english: to tell you: his fire is [liable] because it is like his arrows.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a derivation that began before this section.
steps.raayaObject: The view that אשו משום חציו
steps.raayaSupportSource: The wording of שמות 22:5, which starts with damage by property and ends with damage by the person himself

steps.title: אביי's difficulty: where does the exemption for hidden items fit?
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks: if fire is like arrows, how can there ever be a case where the Torah exempts a person for hidden items (טמון) that his fire burned?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: אביי found this difficult. According to the one who says his fire is like his arrows, how can you find the case of hidden items in a fire that the Torah exempted?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא reports a question that bothered אביי. The question attacks the idea of אשו משום חציו from the rule of טמון באש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If someone shoots an arrow, he pays for whatever it hits, whether it was hidden or out in the open. So if fire is just like arrows, he should pay for hidden items too. But the Torah exempts hidden items burned by fire, so אביי asks how that exemption could ever apply.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the one who says
Hidden items burned in a fire, which the Torah exempts from payment
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah
How can you find such a case?

phrases.english: Rava said,
it was difficult for Abaye:
according to the one who says his fire is [liable] because of his arrows,
hidden items in a fire, which the Merciful One exempted —
how can you find it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the view that was just proven in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view of אשו משום חציו
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Arrows make you liable for hidden and open items alike. So if fire is like arrows, the Torah's exemption for טמון באש seems to have no case where it applies.

steps.title: אביי's answer: the fence fell, so his arrows ran out
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the exemption for hidden items applies when a fire was in one yard and the fence fell for some other reason. The fire then spread to another yard, and at that point his 'arrows' had run out.
steps.simpleTranslation: And אביי was satisfied: for example, a fire broke out in that yard, and a fence fell down not because of the fire, and the fire spread, lit things and caused damage in another yard. There, his arrows have run out.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי resolves his own question by describing a specific case where the exemption for hidden items can apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person's fire was only supposed to stay in his own yard, since a fence blocked it. When the fence fell for a reason that had nothing to do with the fire, the spread into the next yard is no longer his 'arrow'. In that case the liability is not based on arrows, so the exemption for hidden items can apply.

keyTerms.meaning: And it was resolved for him; he found an answer
His arrows have run out; his direct action has ended

steps.confusionAlert: Under this first answer, once 'his arrows have run out' there is nothing left to make him liable for the fire's spread into the other yard. That is exactly why the next step objects that open items (גלוי) should be exempt too.

phrases.english: And it was settled for him:
for example, where a fire broke out in that yard,
and a fence fell, not because of the fire,
and [the fire] went and burned and caused damage in another yard.
For there, his arrows have run out.
phrases.notes: Think of an arrow that has stopped flying: his own action only reached as far as his own yard.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the rule to a specific case (אוקימתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Under אשו משום חציו, there seemed to be no case where the exemption for hidden items could ever apply.
steps.terutzMaskana: The exemption applies where the fence fell for another reason. The fire's spread then is no longer his 'arrows'.

steps.title: Challenge: then open items should be exempt too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on אביי's answer: if the arrows ran out, he should be exempt even for items out in the open (גלוי), not just hidden ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then regarding open items too, his arrows have run out!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks אביי's answer by showing it proves too much.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי's reason, that the arrows ran out, has nothing to do with whether the item was hidden or open. So by his logic, the person should be exempt for open items too. But the Torah's special exemption is only for hidden items, so the answer seems not to fit.

keyTerms.meaning: Open, uncovered items that can be seen

phrases.english: If so,

phrases.aramaic: לְעִנְיַן גָּלוּי נָמֵי כְּלוּ לֵיהּ חִצָּיו!
phrases.english: regarding open items too, his arrows have run out!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's answer about the fallen fence
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The reason 'his arrows ran out' applies just as much to open items. So the Torah's exemption, which is only for hidden items, should not be needed.

steps.title: The 'arrows' view also counts fire as property
steps.stepSummary: A new answer: the one who holds חציו also holds ממונו. The exemption for טמון applies where the fence fell by itself and the owner failed to fix it, so he is liable only because the fire is his property.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the one who says fire is like his arrows also says it is like his property. The case is where he should have fenced the yard again and did not. There it is like his ox that he did not hold back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets aside the problem from step 4 and gives a new answer. Even the person who says fire is like arrows agrees that fire can also make you liable as your property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fence fell for some other reason, so the fire's 'arrow' power has run out. But the owner could have fixed the fence and did not, so he is liable because the fire is his property. That is like an ox he failed to stop. Liability for property follows the rules of fire, so he is exempt for טמון but liable for גלוי.

keyTerms.meaning: His property; liability like damage done by one's animal
Struck it in its face (to hold it back)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the two reasons cancel each other. The 'arrows' reason works when the fire spreads directly. The 'property' reason takes over once the arrows run out, and only the property reason brings the exemption for טמון.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the next question. If both sides agree about ממונו, what are they arguing about?

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לְמַאן דְּאִית לֵיהּ מִשּׁוּם חִצָּיו –
phrases.english: Rather, the one who holds liability because of his arrows
phrases.notes: This is רבי יוחנן, who says fire is like arrows.

phrases.english: also holds liability because of his property;
and for example, where he was able to fence it in
and he did not fence it in;
for there, it is like his ox
and he did not strike it in its face.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לְמַאן דְּאִית לֵיהּ מִשּׁוּם חִצָּיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces אביי's answer, which step 4 knocked down.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case and adds a second basis of liability (ממונו) to the 'arrows' view.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the arrows ran out, there is no liability at all, so the exemption should cover גלוי too.
steps.terutzMaskana: Liability continues as ממונו when he failed to rebuild the fence, and ממונו follows the rules of fire, which exempt טמון.

steps.title: Then what do the two views disagree about?
steps.stepSummary: If the 'arrows' view also accepts 'property', what is the practical difference between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש?
steps.simpleTranslation: But since the one who says 'arrows' also says 'property', what is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the real argument is now. This question sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 made רבי יוחנן agree with ריש לקיש that fire can count as property. That seems to erase their argument, so the גמרא wants to know where they still differ.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them?

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי מֵאַחַר דְּמַאן דְּאִית לֵיהּ מִשּׁוּם חִצָּיו
phrases.english: But since the one who holds liability because of his arrows
also holds liability because of his property,
what is the difference between them?
phrases.notes: Between רבי יוחנן (arrows) and ריש לקיש (property).

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מֵאַחַר דְּמַאן דְּאִית לֵיהּ מִשּׁוּם חִצָּיו אִית לֵיהּ נָמֵי מִשּׁוּם מָמוֹנוֹ מַאי בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Grows out of the answer in step 5, which seemed to erase the argument.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical difference between the 'arrows' view and the 'property' view.

steps.title: The difference is the four extra payments
steps.stepSummary: The views differ on whether the fire's owner pays the four extra payments for injuring a person.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference between them is whether he is obligated in the four payments.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the argument is about a fire that injures a person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If fire is like arrows, it is as if the man himself hurt the person. So he pays the four extra payments, as with any personal injury. If fire is only his property, he pays just for the damage itself, the way an owner pays for damage done by his animal.

keyTerms.meaning: The four extra payments for injuring a person: צער, ריפוי, שבת, בושת

steps.whatToRemember: Both views agree fire can count as property. Only the 'arrows' view also makes the owner pay the four extra payments when fire injures a person.

phrases.english: There is a difference between them:
whether to make him liable for the four payments.
phrases.notes: These are pain, medical costs, lost work time and embarrassment, which a person pays when he injures someone himself.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They differ over the four payments for a person injured by fire. The 'arrows' view requires them.

steps.title: Who pays for the cake?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה ruling on the cake and asks who must pay for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says that for the cake he pays in full. Who is the one obligated?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה about the dog and the coal and asks who pays for the cake. This question sets up the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two people are involved: the owner of the dog that took the cake, and the owner of the coal. The משנה does not say which one pays, so the גמרא asks.

phrases.english: For the cake, he pays, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה. A dog took a cake with a coal on it, ate the cake, and set a stack of grain on fire.

phrases.english: Who is obligated?

steps.triggerLanguage: עַל הַחֲרָרָה מְשַׁלֵּם כּוּ׳ מַאן חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the גמרא returns to the wording of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which person must pay for the cake.

steps.title: The dog's owner pays
steps.stepSummary: The owner of the dog pays for the cake.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the dog's owner pays for the cake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dog ate the cake, so its owner pays for what his animal did.

phrases.english: The owner of the dog.

steps.title: Why not the coal's owner too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges this: the owner of the coal should also be liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let the owner of the coal also be liable!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back and asks why the owner of the coal does not share the payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His coal was part of what happened. If he left it unguarded, he seems to carry some blame as well.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner of the burning coal
But let him also be liable

phrases.english: But let the owner of the coal also be liable!

steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that only the dog's owner pays.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The coal's owner also had a part in the damage, so he should share the liability.

steps.title: He guarded his coal properly
steps.stepSummary: The coal's owner is exempt because he guarded his coal properly.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where he guarded his coal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the coal's owner did his job and guarded the coal, so he is not to blame.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since he guarded the coal properly, the damage came only from the dog. So only the dog's owner pays.
steps.whatToRemember: The dog's owner pays for the cake. The coal's owner is exempt because he guarded his coal.

phrases.english: Where he guarded his coal.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: The coal's owner shares the blame for what the coal caused.
steps.terutzMaskana: He guarded his coal properly, so he is not negligent and is exempt.

steps.title: If the coal was guarded, how did the dog get in?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 11: if the coal's owner guarded properly, how did a dog get to the coal?
steps.simpleTranslation: If the coal's owner guarded his coal properly, what is the dog doing there?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the last answer. If the coal's owner really guarded his coal, a dog should never have reached it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 freed the coal's owner from paying because he guarded his coal. But the dog did reach the coal, and that seems to show the guarding was not good enough. So the excuse from step 11 looks weak.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it doing (literally, 'what does it want')

phrases.english: If it is where he guarded his coal,
what is a dog doing there?
phrases.notes: In other words, a dog getting in shows the place was not really guarded.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי כְּשֶׁשִּׁימֵּר גַּחַלְתּוֹ, מַאי בָּעֵי כֶּלֶב הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the תירוץ of step 11 that the coal's owner guarded properly.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the coal's owner guarded his coal properly
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Proper guarding would have kept the dog out. If the dog got in, the guarding failed.

steps.title: The dog dug its way in
steps.stepSummary: The dog dug under the fence or door, so the owner still counts as having guarded properly.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where the dog dug its way in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with one word: the dog dug its way in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The coal's owner did lock up properly. The dog got in anyway by digging underneath. A break-in like that does not show that the owner's guarding was faulty.

phrases.english: Where it dug through.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: it is defined as one where the dog burrowed in.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dog's entry proves the coal was not properly guarded.
steps.terutzMaskana: The coal was properly guarded. The dog broke in by digging, so the coal's owner is exempt.

steps.title: Ordinary doors are expected to be dug under by dogs
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי בריה דרב כהנא learns from this case that dogs are expected to dig under ordinary doors.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי, the son of רב כהנא, said: This teaches that ordinary doors are considered open to being dug under by a dog.
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרי בריה דרב כהנא draws a lesson from the answer in step 13: digging under doors is normal dog behavior.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this case the dog dug in, and its owner still has to pay for the cake. That means digging under a door counts as ordinary dog behavior, not something strange. So the dog's owner is expected to watch his dog, and the coal's owner, who guarded normally, is not blamed.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not say the door owner was careless. It says the dog's owner should expect his dog to dig, which is why the dog's owner pays and the coal's owner does not.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא:
phrases.english: Rav Mari son of Rav Kahana said:
This is to say that ordinary doors
are open to being dug under by a dog.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא: זֹאת אוֹמֶרֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a general rule from the answer in step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Digging under ordinary doors is normal dog behavior, so the dog's owner is responsible for it.

steps.title: Where did the dog eat the cake?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where exactly the dog ate the cake.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where did it eat the cake?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question about the case. It is setting up the next move by asking where the eating took place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The place matters because eating damage has its own rule about where it must happen. The challenge comes in the next step.

phrases.english: Where did it eat it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ruling of step 9 that the dog's owner pays for the cake and asks where the eating happened.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The location where the dog ate the cake

steps.title: Eating in someone else's stack should not make the owner pay
steps.stepSummary: If the dog ate the cake on a stranger's stack, the dog's owner should not pay, because eating damage only counts in the victim's field.
steps.simpleTranslation: If we say it ate the cake on some other person's stack, we need 'and it consumed in the field of another,' and that is missing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests one possible answer and shows that it fails. If the dog ate the cake on a stranger's stack, the cake's owner could not collect for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק teaches that eating damage is paid only when it happens in the injured person's field. A stranger's stack is not the cake owner's property. So under this reading the dog's owner would not have to pay, but step 9 said he does.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And it consumed in the field of another' (שמות 22:4)

phrases.english: If you say it ate it on some other person's stack,
but we need 'and it consumed in the field of another,'
and that is missing!
phrases.notes: The stranger's stack is not the cake owner's field.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵּימָא דְּאַכְלַהּ בְּגָדִישׁ דְּעָלְמָא, הָא בָּעֵינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries one possible answer to step 15 and shows it clashes with the ruling of step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the dog's owner pays for the cake, if the eating happened on a stranger's stack
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Eating damage is paid only in the victim's field. A stranger's stack does not qualify, so there should be no payment.

steps.title: The dog ate it on the cake owner's own stack
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where the dog ate the cake on the stack of the cake's owner, so the eating happened on the victim's property.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for where it ate it on the stack of the cake's owner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the dog ate the cake on the stack belonging to the cake's owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the eating took place on the injured person's own property. That matches the פסוק 'in the field of another', so the dog's owner must pay for the cake, as step 9 said.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for this case (the case is limited to this)

steps.whatToRemember: The dog's owner pays for the cake only because the dog ate it on the cake owner's own stack. Eating damage counts only in the victim's field.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
for where it ate it on the stack of the cake's owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּאַכְלַהּ בְּגָדִישׁ דְּבַעַל חֲרָרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the stack belongs to the cake's owner.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dog ate the cake on a stranger's stack, so no payment is due for eating.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dog ate the cake on the cake owner's own stack, so the eating damage happened in the victim's field and must be paid.

steps.title: Using this case to settle a question about a cow's mouth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to suggest that this case settles an open question about a cow's mouth.
steps.simpleTranslation: Resolve from here that a cow's mouth...
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא starts to say that this case can answer a question about a cow's mouth, and the full idea continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case was just set on the victim's own property. The גמרא wants to use that detail to answer an earlier open question. The details of the proof come next.

keyTerms.meaning: Resolve (a question that was left open)

phrases.english: Resolve from here that a cow's mouth –

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the case defined in step 17 to try to settle another question.
steps.raayaObject: An open question about the status of a cow's mouth
steps.raayaSupportSource: The case of the dog eating the cake on the cake owner's stack, as defined in step 17
